title: NEC Article 240 — Overcurrent Protection
description: Fuses, circuit breakers, conductor protection, and overcurrent device sizing per NEC 2023 Article 240. 15 questions.

questions.question: Under NEC 2023 Section 240.4, what is the general rule governing the relationship between an overcurrent protective device (OCPD) and the conductor it protects?
choices: The OCPD rating shall not exceed the ampacity of the conductors it protects.
The OCPD rating shall be at least 125% of the conductor ampacity.
The OCPD rating shall not exceed 80% of the conductor ampacity for continuous loads only.
The OCPD rating may be any standard size that is within two sizes of the conductor ampacity.
questions.answer: The OCPD rating shall not exceed the ampacity of the conductors it protects.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4 establishes the general rule that conductors must be protected against overcurrent in accordance with their ampacity — meaning the OCPD rating shall not exceed the ampacity of the conductors it protects. Specific exceptions (such as the next-higher-size rule and small-conductor limits) are addressed in 240.4(B) and 240.4(D).

questions.question: A 6 AWG copper branch circuit conductor has an ampacity of 65 amperes at its 75°C terminal rating. No standard OCPD size of 65A exists. Under NEC 2023 Section 240.4(B), which of the following correctly describes when the next higher standard OCPD size may be used?
choices: The next higher standard size is permitted provided it does not exceed 800 amperes and the conductor does not supply more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads.
The next higher standard size is always permitted regardless of the load type or OCPD rating, as long as the conductor is copper.
The next higher standard size is permitted only when the conductor ampacity exactly equals a standard OCPD rating.
The next higher standard size is permitted only for feeders, never for branch circuits.
questions.answer: The next higher standard size is permitted provided it does not exceed 800 amperes and the conductor does not supply more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(B) permits the next higher standard OCPD rating above the conductor ampacity when three conditions are all met: (1) the conductors do not supply more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads, (2) the conductor ampacity does not exactly correspond to a standard OCPD size, and (3) the next higher standard size selected does not exceed 800 amperes. The 800A ceiling exists because standard OCPD size gaps above 800A become very large, creating unacceptable overprotection gaps.

questions.question: Per NEC 2023 Section 240.4(D), what is the maximum OCPD rating permitted for a 12 AWG copper conductor used as a branch circuit conductor?
choices: 15 amperes
20 amperes
25 amperes
30 amperes
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(D) establishes absolute maximum OCPD ratings for small conductors that cannot be exceeded regardless of the next-higher-size rule in 240.4(B): 14 AWG copper is limited to 15A, 12 AWG copper is limited to 20A, and 10 AWG copper is limited to 30A. For aluminum and copper-clad aluminum, 12 AWG is limited to 15A and 10 AWG to 25A. These limits are fixed and the 240.4(B) round-up rule does not apply.

questions.question: According to NEC 2023 Table 240.6(A), which of the following is a correct list of consecutive standard ampere ratings for fuses and inverse time circuit breakers?
questions.explanation: NEC 240.6(A) lists the standard ampere ratings for fuses and inverse time circuit breakers as: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 600, 700, 800, 1000, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, and 6000 amperes. Note that both 35A and 45A are standard sizes and are often missed on exams. Additional fuse-only standard ratings include 1, 3, 6, 10, and 601 amperes.

questions.question: A luminaire installed in a commercial building contains an internal fuse to protect its LED driver circuitry. How does NEC 2023 Section 240.10 classify this internal fuse, and what does it require?
choices: It is classified as supplementary overcurrent protection; it is not a substitute for required branch-circuit overcurrent protection and does not need to be readily accessible.
It is classified as branch-circuit overcurrent protection and must be readily accessible at all times.
It is classified as a primary overcurrent device and must be rated to match the branch-circuit OCPD.
It is classified as supplementary overcurrent protection and must be rated at no more than 15 amperes.
questions.answer: It is classified as supplementary overcurrent protection; it is not a substitute for required branch-circuit overcurrent protection and does not need to be readily accessible.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.10 states that where supplementary overcurrent protection is used for luminaires, appliances, and other equipment, or for internal circuits and components of equipment, it shall not be used as a substitute for the required branch-circuit overcurrent protection. Supplementary overcurrent devices are also not required to be readily accessible, distinguishing them from standard branch-circuit OCPDs covered by 240.24(A).

questions.question: NEC 2023 Section 240.15(A) requires that a fuse or overcurrent trip unit of a circuit breaker be connected in series with each ungrounded conductor. Which arrangement is specifically permitted as an alternative to a fuse in series with an ungrounded conductor?
choices: A current transformer (CT) with an overcurrent trip relay in lieu of a fuse.
A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) device rated for the circuit load.
A thermal cutout device rated at 125% of the continuous load.
A current-limiting reactor installed at the point of supply.
questions.answer: A current transformer (CT) with an overcurrent trip relay in lieu of a fuse.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.15(A) requires a fuse or an overcurrent trip unit of a circuit breaker to be connected in series with each ungrounded conductor. It also specifically permits using a current transformer (CT) and an overcurrent trip relay in lieu of a fuse as an equivalent means of providing overcurrent protection in series with ungrounded conductors.

questions.question: Per NEC 2023 Section 240.20, which conductors must be protected by an overcurrent device?
choices: Each ungrounded conductor must be protected by an overcurrent device.
Both grounded and ungrounded conductors must each have their own OCPD.
Only the grounded (neutral) conductor requires overcurrent protection.
Only conductors larger than 10 AWG require overcurrent protection.
questions.answer: Each ungrounded conductor must be protected by an overcurrent device.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.20 requires overcurrent protection in each ungrounded conductor. An OCPD is generally not permitted to be connected in series with a grounded (neutral) conductor unless the device opens all conductors of the circuit simultaneously and is designed so that no pole can operate independently, or where motor overload protection under 430.36 or 430.37 requires it.

questions.question: Under NEC 2023 Section 240.21, where must an overcurrent protective device generally be located in a circuit?
choices: At the point where the conductors receive their supply, with specific tap exceptions permitted under 240.21(A) through (H).
At the load end of every conductor run, regardless of circuit type.
At a readily accessible location within 6 feet of the panelboard, unless the circuit exceeds 200 amperes.
At the midpoint of the circuit run for feeder conductors longer than 100 feet.
questions.answer: At the point where the conductors receive their supply, with specific tap exceptions permitted under 240.21(A) through (H).
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21 requires overcurrent protective devices to be located at the point where the conductors receive their supply. This ensures all circuit current is forced through the OCPD. Exceptions are enumerated in 240.21(A) through (H), covering branch circuits, feeder taps, transformer secondary conductors, service conductors, busway taps, motor circuits, generator output conductors, and solar photovoltaic system output circuits. Importantly, a conductor supplied under any of these exceptions cannot in turn supply another conductor except through a properly rated OCPD (the 'you can't tap a tap' principle).

questions.question: An electrician wants to make an indoor feeder tap from a feeder protected by a 400-ampere OCPD. The tap conductors will be 8 feet long and terminate in a single circuit breaker. Per NEC 2023 Section 240.21(B)(1), what is the minimum ampacity the tap conductors must have?
choices: At least 40 amperes (one-tenth of 400A) or the ampacity required for the load served, whichever is greater.
At least 133 amperes (one-third of 400A), and they must be installed in a raceway.
At least 200 amperes (one-half of 400A) to provide adequate short-circuit protection.
At least 400 amperes, matching the upstream feeder OCPD rating.
questions.answer: At least 40 amperes (one-tenth of 400A) or the ampacity required for the load served, whichever is greater.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(B)(1) covers indoor feeder taps not exceeding 10 feet. The tap conductors must have an ampacity of not less than the combined calculated loads and not less than the rating of the device (OCPD or equipment) supplied by the tap — but at minimum, the ampacity must be at least one-tenth (1/10) of the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder conductors. For a 400A feeder OCPD, this yields a minimum of 40A. The conductors must also terminate in a single OCPD, be protected from physical damage (e.g., installed in a raceway), and the 240.4(B) round-up rule is prohibited for tap conductors.

questions.question: A 25-foot indoor feeder tap is made from a feeder protected by a 600-ampere overcurrent device. Per NEC 2023 Section 240.21(B)(2), what is the minimum ampacity the tap conductors must have, and how must they terminate?
choices: At least 200 amperes (one-third of 600A); they must terminate in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses rated no higher than the tap conductor's ampacity.
At least 60 amperes (one-tenth of 600A); they must terminate in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses.
At least 300 amperes (one-half of 600A); they may terminate in a panelboard with multiple branch circuit breakers.
At least 400 amperes (two-thirds of 600A); they must terminate in a single OCPD rated to match the feeder.
questions.answer: At least 200 amperes (one-third of 600A); they must terminate in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses rated no higher than the tap conductor's ampacity.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(B)(2) permits feeder tap conductors not exceeding 25 feet under these conditions: (1) the tap conductor ampacity must be not less than one-third (1/3) the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder — for a 600A feeder, that is 200A minimum; (2) the tap conductors must terminate in a single circuit breaker or a single set of fuses rated no higher than the tap conductor's ampacity; (3) the tap conductors must be protected from physical damage by being enclosed in a raceway. Unlike the 10-foot tap, the 1/3 calculation is based on the feeder's OCPD rating, not the feeder conductor ampacity.

questions.question: NEC 2023 Section 240.24(A) requires overcurrent protective devices to be readily accessible. Which of the following installation scenarios violates this requirement?
choices: A panelboard installed in a utility room that requires moving stored boxes to reach the breaker handles.
A panelboard installed in an electrical room that is kept locked but accessible to qualified persons with a key.
A circuit breaker installed in a surface-mounted enclosure at 5 feet above the finished floor.
A fusible disconnect installed on the exterior wall of a commercial building behind a hinged cover.
questions.answer: A panelboard installed in a utility room that requires moving stored boxes to reach the breaker handles.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(A) requires that overcurrent devices be readily accessible, meaning capable of being reached quickly for operation, renewal, or inspection without requiring a ladder or the removal of obstacles. A panelboard blocked by stored items is not readily accessible because obstacles must be removed to reach it. A locked electrical room accessible to qualified persons with a key is generally considered readily accessible. Note that 240.24(A) also limits the height of the highest overcurrent device handle to not more than 2.0 m (6 ft 7 in.) above the floor or working platform.

questions.question: A contractor is planning to install a panelboard in a stairwell so it is centrally located for both floors. Per NEC 2023 Section 240.24(F), which of the following is true?
choices: Overcurrent devices shall not be located over steps of a stairway.
Overcurrent devices may be located over steps if the panel handle height does not exceed 5 feet above any step.
Overcurrent devices are permitted over steps only if they are supplementary overcurrent devices.
Overcurrent devices may be located over steps provided a permanent platform is installed in front of the panel.
questions.answer: Overcurrent devices shall not be located over steps of a stairway.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(F) flatly prohibits locating overcurrent devices over steps of a stairway. This is a safety rule: operating or resetting a breaker while standing on steps creates a fall hazard. The prohibition applies to standard overcurrent protective devices; supplementary overcurrent protection (addressed separately in 240.10) has different accessibility requirements, but the over-steps rule in 240.24(F) applies to required OCPDs.

questions.question: Per NEC 2023 Sections 240.51 and 240.54, regarding Edison-base plug fuses and Type S fuses, which statement is correct?
choices: Edison-base plug fuses are permitted only as replacements in existing installations where there is no evidence of overfusing or tampering; Type S adapters installed in Edison-base fuseholders cannot be removed once inserted.
Edison-base plug fuses may be used in new installations provided the circuit does not exceed 30 amperes and 125 volts.
Type S fuses are fully interchangeable with Edison-base fuses of the same ampere rating without adapters.
Edison-base fuseholders may accept Type S fuses of a higher ampere rating in an emergency, provided the conductor is properly derated.
questions.answer: Edison-base plug fuses are permitted only as replacements in existing installations where there is no evidence of overfusing or tampering; Type S adapters installed in Edison-base fuseholders cannot be removed once inserted.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.51(B) restricts Edison-base plug fuses to replacement use only in existing installations where there is no evidence of overfusing or tampering — they are not permitted in new installations. NEC 240.54 requires that Edison-base fuseholders be made to accept Type S fuses through the use of non-removable adapters. Once inserted, Type S adapters cannot be removed (240.54(C)), preventing overfusing by making it impossible to install a higher-rated fuse. Plug fuses are classified at not more than 125 volts and 30 amperes per 240.50(A).

questions.question: Per NEC 2023 Section 240.80, what indication must a circuit breaker provide regarding its operational status?
choices: The circuit breaker must clearly indicate whether it is in the open (off), closed (on), or tripped position.
The circuit breaker must only indicate whether the circuit is energized or de-energized via a built-in pilot light.
The circuit breaker must display the amount of current flowing through the circuit on a digital readout.
The circuit breaker must provide an audible alarm when it trips to an open position.
questions.answer: The circuit breaker must clearly indicate whether it is in the open (off), closed (on), or tripped position.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.80 (Method of Operation) requires circuit breakers to be capable of being operated manually and to clearly indicate whether the breaker is in the open (off), closed (on), or tripped position. This three-state indication is critical for safe operation and troubleshooting — a tripped breaker must be visually distinguishable from a breaker that has been manually opened, so workers can identify fault conditions. Circuit breakers may also include shunt trips or remote operators in addition to manual operation.

questions.question: NEC 2023 Section 240.85 permits circuit breakers to be applied in series-rated combinations. Which of the following correctly describes a key requirement for using a series-rated system?
choices: The series combination must be tested and listed; the equipment must be field-marked with a caution label stating the series combination rating in amperes and that identified replacement components are required.
Any circuit breaker may be used in a series combination as long as the upstream OCPD has an AIC rating at least twice that of the downstream breaker.
Series-rated systems require no special labeling provided the upstream device has a higher AIC rating than the available fault current.
Series ratings are only permitted in existing installations selected by a licensed electrical engineer and are prohibited in new construction.
questions.answer: The series combination must be tested and listed; the equipment must be field-marked with a caution label stating the series combination rating in amperes and that identified replacement components are required.
questions.explanation: NEC 240.85 permits circuit breakers to be used in series-rated combinations where the downstream breaker's individual AIC rating is lower than the available fault current, provided the specific combination has been tested and listed. Per NEC 110.22(C), equipment enclosures containing OCPDs used in a series combination must be legibly field-marked with: 'CAUTION — SERIES COMBINATION SYSTEM RATED ___ AMPERES. IDENTIFIED REPLACEMENT COMPONENTS REQUIRED.' This label alerts maintenance personnel that only specific replacement OCPDs may be used to maintain the tested series rating. The series combination rating cannot exceed the AIC rating of the upstream device.
